datasheet.motivation: A single government release covered by six outlets on the same day. Chosen because a ground-truth primary source exists, which makes claim-level comparison checkable rather than interpretive.
datasheet.outlet_selection_rule: Six US outlets that published original coverage of the June 2026 Employment Situation release within 24 hours, spanning wire-style business press, broadcast news, cable news, public radio, and a policy think tank. Selected by the designer. This is a convenience sample, not a representative one.
datasheet.collection_method: Each article was retrieved over the open web and read in full. Every sentence recorded below was copied verbatim from the live page. No sentence was paraphrased, reconstructed, or generated.
datasheet.known_limits: Three of six articles were edited after publication (see revision_notes). Sentences here reflect the version live on the retrieval date, not the version published on July 2.
datasheet.excluded: Reuters, the Associated Press, and The New York Times were attempted and blocked automated retrieval. They were excluded rather than quoted from secondhand summaries.

outlets.name: Fox Business
outlets.headline_live: US economy added jobs at a slower pace than expected in June
outlets.headline_meta: June 2026 jobs report: US economy added jobs at a steady pace
outlets.length_note: Full report, roughly 900 words, with sector-by-sector breakdown.

outlets.name: ABC News
outlets.headline_live: Hiring worse than expected in June, but White House says labor market on 'upward trajectory'
outlets.length_note: Shorter general-audience piece. Covers the headline numbers and the political reaction, not the technical detail.

outlets.name: Center for American Progress
outlets.headline_live: June Jobs Numbers Are Not the Boost for Workers That Was Expected
outlets.length_note: Think tank analysis, not a news report. Written to argue a position about worker outcomes.

outlets.name: CNN
outlets.headline_live: Steady but not strong: US job growth slowed in June
outlets.length_note: Full report with economist quotes and market context.

outlets.name: CNBC
outlets.headline_live: U.S. job creation cools in June with payrolls growth of just 57,000; unemployment rate at 4.2%
outlets.length_note: Written against the forecast. Leads with the miss versus consensus.

outlets.name: NPR
outlets.headline_live: June gloom for the job market as employers add just 57,000 jobs
outlets.format_note: All Things Considered radio transcript, not a written article. Several omissions below follow from that format.
outlets.length_note: All Things Considered segment, roughly three minutes of audio. Carries far fewer claims than any written piece, by format.

revision_notes: Fox Business: the live H1 reads 'slower pace than expected' while the page title and opening body sentence still read 'steady pace'. Published 08:31, updated 10:45 the same day.
ABC News: a syndicated copy preserves an earlier version giving May as 172,000; the live version gives 129,000. Published 2026-07-02, modified 2026-07-03.
CNBC: carries an explicit correction note reading 'Correction: The unemployment rate was 4.3% in May. An earlier version mischaracterized the recent trend.' Published 08:31, updated 12:50.
CNN: published 05:00, updated 11:42, no correction note.
NPR: dateModified equals datePublished. No evidence of revision.

sentences.fox: The Bureau of Labor Statistics on Thursday reported that employers added 57,000 jobs in June.
sentences.abc: The U.S. added 57,000 jobs in June, according to the federal government's monthly jobs report, which marked a decline from 129,000 jobs added in May.
sentences.cap: The labor market added 57,000 jobs, coming in well below expectations, and job growth over the prior two months was revised down by 74,000.
sentences.cnn: US job growth settled down after a spring surge, as employers added a lower-than-expected 57,000 positions last month, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Thursday.
sentences.cnbc: Nonfarm payrolls for June increased by a seasonally adjusted 57,000 for the month, slower than the downwardly revised 129,000 added in May and worse than the 115,000 Dow Jones consensus forecast.
sentences.npr: U.S. employers added only 57,000 jobs in June.

claims.text: The unemployment rate fell to 4.2 percent

sentences.fox: The unemployment rate dipped to 4.2%, which was also below the estimate of 4.3%.
sentences.abc: The unemployment rate fell slightly from 4.3% in May to 4.2% in June, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said.
sentences.cap: The unemployment rate dropped slightly to 4.2 percent, but this was entirely driven by people leaving the labor force rather than moving into employment.
sentences.cnn: Thursday's data also showed that the unemployment rate dropped to 4.2% from 4.3% as more people left the labor force.
sentences.cnbc: The unemployment rate, however, dropped to 4.2%, slightly ahead of the 4.1% where it was a year ago.
sentences.npr: People who are not looking for work don't count as unemployed, and that's why the jobless rate inched down to 4.2%.

claims.text: Hiring came in below what economists expected
claims.divergence_note: All six say the number missed expectations. They do not agree on what was expected. CNBC cites 115,000 from Dow Jones, Fox Business cites 110,000 from an LSEG poll, CNN cites 100,000 without naming a provider, and ABC, CAP and NPR give no figure at all.

sentences.fox: That figure was below the estimate of economists polled by LSEG, who estimated 110,000 jobs added.
sentences.abc: Hiring slowed markedly in June, falling short of economists' expectations and displaying a wobbly labor market amid elevated inflation set off by the Iran war.
sentences.cap: The labor market added 57,000 jobs, coming in well below expectations, and job growth over the prior two months was revised down by 74,000.
sentences.cnn: Economists, by consensus, had expected a total of 100,000 jobs added in June and a jobless rate remaining at 4.3% for the fourth consecutive month.
sentences.cnbc: Nonfarm payrolls for June increased by a seasonally adjusted 57,000 for the month, slower than the downwardly revised 129,000 added in May and worse than the 115,000 Dow Jones consensus forecast.
sentences.npr: U.S. employers added fewer jobs than expected last month.

claims.text: The unemployment rate fell because people left the labor force, not because more people found work

state_notes.fox: Reports the participation decline as a separate fact and never connects it to the falling unemployment rate.
state_notes.abc: Does not mention the labor force participation decline at all.
state_notes.cnbc: States it unambiguously in the article's key-points list. In the body the antecedent of 'The move lower' is ambiguous after a post-publication edit.

sentences.fox: The labor force participation rate decreased by 0.3 percentage points to 61.5% in June, while the employment-population ratio edged down by 0.2 percentage points to 59%.
sentences.cap: The unemployment rate dropped slightly to 4.2 percent, but this was entirely driven by people leaving the labor force rather than moving into employment.
sentences.cnn: Not only were employment gains softer in June, but the unemployment rate dropped as fewer people were in the labor market.
sentences.cnbc: The unemployment rate, however, dropped to 4.2%, largely due to a slump in the labor force participation rate, which fell 0.3 percentage point to 61.5%, the lowest since March 2021.
sentences.npr: The unemployment rate fell, but only because a large number of people stopped looking for work.

claims.text: Payrolls for April and May were revised down by a combined 74,000

state_notes.cnbc: Gives the two components, 43,000 for May and 31,000 for April, but never states the combined 74,000 total.

sentences.fox: Taken together, employment in April and May was 74,000 jobs lower than previously reported.
sentences.cap: The labor market added 57,000 jobs, coming in well below expectations, and job growth over the prior two months was revised down by 74,000.
sentences.cnn: Monthly totals for April and May were revised down by a combined 74,000 jobs, to 148,000 and 129,000, respectively.
sentences.cnbc: Prior months also saw significant downward revisions — the May total, which had been much stronger than economists had anticipated, was cut by 43,000, while April's figure came down 31,000 to 148,000 as the report showed labor market growth significantly slower than previously thought.
sentences.npr: And what's more, the jobs numbers for April and May were revised down, wiping out a total of 74,000 jobs we thought were added during the two previous months.

claims.text: Labor force participation fell to 61.5 percent

state_notes.cap: Refers to people leaving the labor force but never gives the participation rate.
state_notes.npr: Not mentioned in either NPR piece.

sentences.fox: The labor force participation rate decreased by 0.3 percentage points to 61.5% in June, while the employment-population ratio edged down by 0.2 percentage points to 59%.
sentences.cnn: Labor force participation dropped to a five-year low of 61.5% last month, falling from 61.8% in May.
sentences.cnbc: The move lower was largely due to a slump in the labor force participation rate, which dropped 0.3 percentage point to 61.5%, the lowest since March 2021.

claims.text: Average hourly earnings rose 3.5 percent from a year earlier

sentences.cap: In comparison, the June jobs report shows that nominal wages grew 3.5 percent from the prior year.
sentences.cnn: Workers' annual pay gains, which registered at 3.5% in June, are being entirely eaten away, and then some, by inflation, which rose at a 4.2% clip in May.
sentences.cnbc: Average hourly earnings rose 0.3% for the month and 3.5% from a year ago, both in line with the consensus forecasts.
sentences.npr: Average wages in June were up 3.5% from a year ago.

state_notes.cap: Says hiring was below average in leisure and hospitality but gives no job-loss figure.
state_notes.npr: The main transcript says only that restaurants and retailers cut jobs. A companion NPR piece gives the 61,000 figure.

sentences.fox: Leisure and hospitality employment declined by 61,000 in June, which reflected weaker than usual seasonal hiring.
sentences.cap: June 2026 data even show that hiring was below average in low-wage industries that have driven the labor market growth over the past year, such as the health care and leisure and hospitality industries.
sentences.cnn: Thursday's report showed that leisure and hospitality businesses shed 61,000 jobs last month, a reflection of weaker-than-usual seasonal hiring, the BLS noted in the report.
sentences.cnbc: However, leisure and hospitality reported a loss of 61,000 jobs, which the BLS said reflected slower-than-usual seasonal hiring.
sentences.npr: Restaurants and retailers cut jobs last month.

claims.text: Job growth over the past year was concentrated in low-wage industries

state_notes.npr: A companion NPR piece attributes part of the wage-growth uptick to low-wage jobs disappearing, which is a related but different claim.

sentences.cap: The data also showed that job growth over the past year was concentrated in low-wage industries.
sentences.npr: That is a slightly bigger annual increase than the previous month, but that improvement is probably at least partly the result of a lot of low-wage leisure and hospitality jobs drying up last month.

claims.text: Professional and business services led job gains, adding 36,000

state_notes.general: Recorded as 1/6 because only the ABC sentence was verified verbatim. Other outlets may cover this; it was not confirmed and is therefore not counted.

sentences.abc: The professional and business services sector led job gains in June, adding 36,000 positions.

pairs.full: The U.S. economy added jobs at a steady pace in June despite headwinds caused by elevated inflation and uncertainty over the Iran war's economic impact.

pairs.phrase: settled down after a spring surge
pairs.full: US job growth settled down after a spring surge, as employers added a lower-than-expected 57,000 positions last month, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Thursday.
U.S. employers added only 57,000 jobs in June.
Hiring slowed markedly in June, falling short of economists' expectations and displaying a wobbly labor market amid elevated inflation set off by the Iran war.

panel.rule: The panel is chosen per story, not fixed across the site. For this story the panel is outlets that ran original coverage of the BLS release within 24 hours, spanning a business desk, a markets desk, general broadcast news, public radio, and a policy think tank.
panel.why_these: A jobs report is covered by business and economics desks. A sports story or a health story would draw a completely different panel, and the counts on this page would mean nothing if applied to one.
panel.who_chose: The panel was chosen by the designer, Milan Khanal. No outlet was excluded for what it said. Reuters, the Associated Press, and The New York Times were attempted and blocked automated retrieval, so they were left out rather than quoted secondhand.
panel.the_catch: Panel size decides what agreement looks like. Six outlets make unanimity easy; thirty would make it rare. Every count on this page is relative to these six and to nothing wider. This is the most consequential judgment NewsLens makes and it is not made by the AI.
panel.not_yet_built: Readers cannot currently add or remove an outlet and watch the counts change. That is the single most important missing feature, because it is the one that would hand this judgment to the reader.
